claim: A sunscreen's SPF is not a percentage of protection; doubling SPF does not double the share of UVB blocked.
source_title: 21 CFR 352.3, Definitions (US sunscreen monograph): SPF, MED, 2 mg/cm² test application
note: Follows from the definition (c2) and the AAD's figures (c3). Badge 'model' on the rays.

claim: SPF is defined as the ratio of the UV dose needed to produce the minimal erythema dose (first perceptible redness) on protected skin to that on unprotected skin.
source_title: 21 CFR 352.3, Definitions (US sunscreen monograph): SPF, MED, 2 mg/cm² test application
note: Excerpt: SPF is the ratio of the UV energy needed to cause an MED on protected skin to that on unprotected skin; MED(PS) is measured after applying 2 mg/cm² of the product.

sentence: It's a ratio: how much more burning light your skin can take under the film before it reddens.
source_title: 21 CFR 352.3, Definitions (US sunscreen monograph): SPF, MED, 2 mg/cm² test application

sentence: Flip it, and fifty lets through about a fiftieth of that light, a hundred about a hundredth, which is barely more blocked.
claim: Under the idealised reading of SPF, a product transmits about 1/SPF of sunburning UV: SPF 50 about 2% (≈98% blocked), SPF 100 about 1% (≈99% blocked).
source_title: AAD survey shows Americans need sunscreen education (American Academy of Dermatology)
note: AAD: SPF 30 blocks 97% of UVB; higher SPFs block slightly more, none blocks 100%. SPF 50 ≈ 98% is widely given citing the AAD; 99% for SPF 100 is computed (1 − 1/100). The 1/SPF transmission is an idealisation (the SPF test is a sunburn ratio, not a transmission measurement); badged 'model'. On screen: 98% · 99%, 2% · 1%.

sentence: But look at what gets in, and the bigger number lets in half as much, as long as the film is as thick as the lab's.
claim: Under the same idealisation, SPF 100 transmits about half the sunburning UV that SPF 50 does (1/100 vs 1/50), at the test application of 2 mg/cm².
source_title: 21 CFR 352.3, Definitions (US sunscreen monograph): SPF, MED, 2 mg/cm² test application
note: Computed: (1/100) ÷ (1/50) = 0.5. Valid at the test's 2 mg/cm² layer (c5).

sentence: But look at what gets in, and the bigger number lets in half as much, as long as the film is as thick as the lab's.
claim: SPF is measured with 2 mg/cm² of product applied.
source_title: 21 CFR 352.3, Definitions (US sunscreen monograph): SPF, MED, 2 mg/cm² test application
note: Excerpt: MED(PS) after application of 2 milligrams per square centimeter of the final formulation.

sentence: Real people, studies found, spread a quarter to half as much as the lab, and protection falls well below the label, by an amount still argued over.
claim: Studies of real-world use find people apply about 0.39–1.0 mg/cm², roughly a fifth to a half of the 2 mg/cm² test amount.
source_title: Petersen B, Wulf HC (2014). Application of sunscreen: theory and reality. Photodermatol Photoimmunol Photomed 30:96–101
note: Excerpt (secondary, describing the review): real-life application of 0.39 to 1.0 mg/cm². Said as 'a quarter to half', the central range; '0.4–1 mg/cm²' on screen. A 2023 imaging study found 1.04 mg/cm² without guidance (search excerpt).

sentence: Real people, studies found, spread a quarter to half as much as the lab, and protection falls well below the label, by an amount still argued over.
claim: Applying less than 2 mg/cm² gives an SPF well below the labelled value; whether the fall is roughly proportional or steeper (exponential) is disputed.
source_title: Faurschou A, Wulf HC (2007). The relation between sun protection factor and amount of sunscreen applied in vivo. Br J Dermatol 156:716–719
note: Faurschou & Wulf 2007 (SPF 4 product): exponential relation, SPF far lower at 0.5 and 1 mg/cm². BASF's commentary cites a German multicenter study: about a quarter of the labelled SPF at 0.5 mg/cm² and about half at 1.0 mg/cm² (closer to linear). Both agree it falls well below the label; badge 'debated'.

sentence: That lab layer is about as thick as the dead layer under it, a fifth of a sheet of paper.
claim: 2 mg/cm² of a product with a density near 1 g/cm³ is a layer about 20 µm thick.
source_title: 21 CFR 352.3, Definitions (US sunscreen monograph): SPF, MED, 2 mg/cm² test application
note: Computed: 2 mg/cm² ÷ 1 g/cm³ = 2×10⁻³ cm = 20 µm. The FDA monograph's test spreads 100 mg or 100 µl over 50 cm², assuming a specific gravity of 1 (search excerpt). Real films are uneven; 'about'.

sentence: That lab layer is about as thick as the dead layer under it, a fifth of a sheet of paper.
claim: The cheek's stratum corneum is about 17 µm (16.8 µm) and copy paper about 100 µm; 20 µm is about a fifth of the paper.
source_title: Egawa M, Hirao T, Takahashi M (2007). In vivo estimation of stratum corneum thickness … Acta Derm Venereol 87:4–8
note: Ep01 c12/c13. Computed 20/100 = 0.2 (on screen: ≈20 µm · 17 µm · 100 µm).

sentence: So the bigger number doesn't block twice as much.
claim: SPF 100 does not block twice as much UVB as SPF 50 (about 99% vs 98%) (restates c3).
source_title: AAD survey shows Americans need sunscreen education (American Academy of Dermatology)

sentence: It lets half as much in, when there's enough of it.
claim: At the test thickness SPF 100 lets about half as much sunburning UV through as SPF 50; with too little product neither reaches its label (restates c4 and c7).
source_title: 21 CFR 352.3, Definitions (US sunscreen monograph): SPF, MED, 2 mg/cm² test application
note: Restates c4, c7. A dermatologist checks it reads as how the numbers work, not as advice.
